## TITLE

**"Deterministic Target Leakage in Photovoltaic Forecasting: A Ten-Location
Empirical Quantification and Climate-Aware Forecastability Assessment
Across Six Indonesian Climate Regimes"**

---

## KEYWORDS

Photovoltaic forecasting; Deterministic target leakage; Stochastic target
reconstruction; Walk-forward validation; Maritime Continent; Multi-site
generalisation; OLS-HC3; XGBoost; SARIMAX; SHAP; NASA POWER; Meta-analysis;
Reproducibility

---

## ABSTRACT

Deterministic target construction — expressing a photovoltaic (PV) output
target as an algebraic function of predictor variables — produces apparent
R² values approaching unity that reflect formula recovery rather than
forecasting skill. We provide a ten-location empirical quantification of
this leakage pathology across six climate regimes of the Indonesian
archipelago: equatorial wet (Medan, Pekanbaru), equatorial maritime
(Pontianak, Bontang, Samarinda, Balikpapan), monsoonal (Makassar),
tropical monsoon (Surabaya), semi-arid tropical (Kupang), and equatorial
rainforest (Jayapura). Using 21-year NASA POWER monthly datasets
(2005–2025, n = 252 per site), deterministic target construction yields
R²_det ≈ 0.9999–1.0000 universally across all ten locations. Stochastic
target reconstruction reduces R² substantially at every site, with
leakage ratios (R²_det/R²_stoch) ranging from 1.72× (Makassar) to 3.43×
(Pontianak), and a Spearman rank correlation of ρ = −0.903 (permutation
p = 0.0007, n = 10) confirming a systematic inverse relationship between
local GHI variability and leakage magnitude.

A fixed-effects meta-analysis of GHI anomaly coefficients across all ten
sites yields a pooled estimate of β = +0.102 kWh/m²/day (z = 15.28,
p ≪ 10⁻⁶; 95% CI: [0.089, 0.115]) with near-zero between-site
heterogeneity (I² = 0.0%, p_Q = 0.851), indicating that the marginal
effect of irradiance anomaly on PV output is quantitatively stable
across six fundamentally different climate regimes. Using leakage-free
per-fold expanding-window climatological baselines, XGBoost significantly
outperforms climatology at three of ten sites (Balikpapan p = 0.002,
Bontang p = 0.010, Makassar p = 0.037); a between-site Kruskal-Wallis
test (H = 9.000, p = 0.437) confirms that the across-site variation in
forecastability is not statistically distinguishable from within-site
sampling variance. SHAP analysis identifies GHI_anom as the dominant [10]
predictor at six of ten sites; the thermal-humidity interaction (T2M×RH)
emerges as rank-1 at Makassar and Surabaya, while Medan and Kupang show
distinct rank-1 features (GHI×CLOUD and GHI_lag12 respectively) —
indicating that feature dominance is majority- but not universally-
consistent across climate regimes. OLS-HC3 and XGBoost are statistically
equivalent at every site. We release an open-source, auto-discovery
pipeline in which adding a new site requires only placing one NASA POWER
CSV into `data/raw/` — no code changes.

---

## 1. INTRODUCTION

### 1.1 Motivation

Data-driven PV forecasting studies routinely report goodness-of-fit
values (R² > 0.90) that appear to confirm the predictability of solar
PV output. A methodological issue that has received insufficient
attention is the construction of the target variable itself: when
Y = η·A·GHI·(1 − β_T·ΔT) and GHI is simultaneously a formula input and
a primary predictor, any regression algorithm trivially recovers the
algebraic identity. We term this phenomenon deterministic target leakage
— applying the established machine-learning concept of target
contamination [1] to the domain of energy forecasting.

### 1.2 Knowledge Gap

Prior single-site studies can characterise the leakage phenomenon at
individual locations but cannot determine whether leakage magnitude is
site-specific or universal. A systematic multi-site study spanning
diverse climate regimes is required to: (i) establish whether the
leakage ratio is a universal constant or a climate-dependent quantity;
(ii) quantify the relationship between local irradiance variability and
leakage magnitude; and (iii) determine whether feature-importance
patterns replicate across climatically distinct sites. Indonesia's
archipelago, spanning 47° of longitude and six distinct climate regimes,
provides a natural laboratory for this purpose. This gap is particularly consequential given growing evidence that ENSO conditions modulate PV output at both global [2] and Indonesian regional scales [3], yet no existing study has quantified whether a leakage-diagnosis methodology itself remains valid — or its magnitude stable — across the climate diversity within a single ENSO-affected archipelago.

### 1.3 Contributions

**(C1 — Primary)** First ten-site, six-climate-regime empirical
quantification of deterministic target leakage: leakage ratio range
1.72×–3.43×; Spearman ρ = −0.903 (n = 10, permutation p = 0.0007)
confirms a systematic inverse relationship between local GHI variance
and leakage magnitude.

**(C2 — Primary)** Meta-analytic synthesis (n = 10) demonstrating that
GHI anomaly's marginal effect on PV output is quantitatively stable
across all six climate regimes (pooled β = +0.102, I² = 0.0%).

**(C3 — Illustrative, site-dependent)** Forecastability characterisation:
XGBoost outperforms climatology at 3/10 sites; between-site variation is
not statistically confirmed (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.437).

**(C4 — Illustrative, majority-consistent)** Attribution: GHI_anom
dominates SHAP rank-1 at 6/10 sites; thermal-humidity interaction
(T2M×RH) dominates at 2/10 sites (Makassar, Surabaya); two sites (Medan,
Kupang) show distinct rank-1 features not predicted by climate regime
alone, motivating caution against assuming universal feature dominance.

**(C5)** Reproducible auto-discovery pipeline: adding a new site requires
only placing its NASA POWER CSV in `data/raw/`.

## 2. STUDY AREA AND DATA

### 2.1 Study Area

Table 1 summarises the ten study locations. The sites span five
Indonesian major island groups (Sumatra, Kalimantan, Sulawesi, Java,
Nusa Tenggara, Papua) and six approximate climate regimes, deliberately
selected to test whether leakage and forecastability findings replicate
across fundamentally different radiation environments.

The GHI standard deviation ranges from 0.353 (Pekanbaru, equatorial wet)
to 0.767 (Kupang, semi-arid tropical) — a factor of 2.17× in irradiance
variability — enabling the systematic detection of the relationship
between climate variance and leakage magnitude reported in Section 4.1.
Cloud fraction ranges from 55.1% (Kupang) to 89.3% (Medan), and
precipitation from 4.13 mm/day (Kupang) to 9.97 mm/day (Medan),
confirming that the ten-site sample spans genuinely distinct radiation
and moisture environments rather than climatic replicates of a single
regime.

### 2.2 NASA POWER Data Source

Monthly Level-3 meteorological data were retrieved from the NASA
Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources (POWER) API (MERRA-2 reanalysis
base with CERES SYN1deg radiation products) for January 2005 through
December 2025, using identical settings across all ten sites: Renewable
Energy user community, UTC time standard, 10 m wind elevation, Savanna
wind surface classification, zero pressure correction. Twelve core
meteorological parameters are present at every site (GHI, DNI, DIFF, KT,
CLOUD, PRECTOT, RH, T2M, TS, WS, WSC, PS); two additional parameters
(PSC at Bontang; T2M_MAX/T2M_MIN at the remaining nine sites) vary by
site due to NASA POWER's site-dependent optional parameter availability
but are not used in the modelling feature set. NASA POWER radiation
products have been independently validated against ground-based
measurements in tropical climates comparable to this study's setting
[4].

---

## 3. METHODOLOGY

### 3.1 Deterministic Target and Leakage Mechanism

Standard PV output estimation follows Y_det = η·A·GHI·(1 − β_T·(T2m −
T_ref)) with η = 0.18, A = 1.0 m², β_T = 0.004/°C, T_ref = 25°C. Because
GHI and T2m are the formula's algebraic inputs and simultaneously the
primary predictors, any model achieves R² → 1 by algebraic recovery.
This construction is applied identically at all ten sites, isolating
site-to-site leakage variation to genuine differences in local GHI/T2m
statistics rather than methodological inconsistency.

### 3.2 Stochastic Target Reconstruction

A physically parameterised (not measured) stochastic target Y_stoch
replaces the deterministic multiplicative structure with seven
independent loss components (thermal derating, cloud-driven residual
attenuation, aerosol scattering, humidity-driven soiling, inverter
efficiency, seasonal/monsoon variability, ENSO-cloud coupling) applied
identically at every site with fixed random seed (42).

### 3.3 Feature Engineering (Leakage-Free)

Twelve predictors are constructed per site: seasonal encoders (sin/cos
month), GHI persistence lags (1, 12 months), climatological anomalies
(GHI, CLOUD, PRECTOT — computed per walk-forward fold from the training
window only, never from the full sample), ENSO index (ONI, lag-2), and
two interaction terms (GHI×CLOUD, T2M×RH, plus ONI×CLOUD_anom). The
per-fold (not full-sample) anomaly computation is the pipeline's central
leakage-prevention mechanism, verified via `utils.verify_no_feature_leakage()`
at every fold, every site.

### 3.4 Models and Evaluation

Three model classes are fit identically at every site: OLS with
HC3-robust standard errors (both a full 12-feature specification for
diagnostics and a low-VIF 8-feature specification for primary
inference), gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost [5];
hyperparameters selected via inner validation on fold-1 only), and
SARIMAX [6] with the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI) [7] as exogenous regressor. Walk-forward
evaluation uses 9 expanding-window folds (train 2005→{2014...2022},
test {2015...2023}) against a leakage-free per-fold expanding-window
climatological baseline; the
final 2024–2025 window is reserved as an unused holdout. Model
comparisons use the Diebold-Mariano test [8] for
pairwise point-forecast equivalence and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test [9]
for paired fold-level skill against climatology.

## 4. RESULTS

### 4.1 Leakage Quantification — 10 Sites (Primary Finding)

**Table 2. Deterministic Leakage Demonstration — All 10 Locations (sorted ascending by leakage ratio)**

| Location | Regime | R²_det | R²_stoch | Leakage Ratio | GHI SD |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Makassar | Monsoonal | 0.999991 | 0.5803 | **1.723× (min)** | 0.757 |
| Kupang | Semi-Arid Tropical | 0.999979 | 0.5345 | 1.871× | 0.767 |
| Surabaya | Tropical Monsoon | 0.999969 | 0.4527 | 2.209× | 0.593 |
| Samarinda | Equatorial Maritime | 0.999996 | 0.3910 | 2.557× | 0.455 |
| Medan | Equatorial Wet | 0.999995 | 0.3695 | 2.706× | 0.425 |
| Bontang | Equatorial Maritime | 0.999997 | 0.3353 | 2.982× | 0.407 |
| Pekanbaru | Equatorial Wet | 0.999996 | 0.3281 | 3.048× | 0.353 |
| Balikpapan | Equatorial Maritime | 0.999997 | 0.3215 | 3.110× | 0.389 |
| Jayapura | Equatorial Rainforest | 0.999997 | 0.3132 | 3.193× | 0.395 |
| Pontianak | Equatorial Maritime | 0.999997 | 0.2912 | **3.434× (max)** | 0.373 |
| **Range** | — | 0.9999–1.0000 | 0.2912–0.5803 | **1.723×–3.434×** | — |

Deterministic target construction yields R²_det ≈ 0.9999–1.0000 at all
ten locations across six climate regimes, confirming that this leakage
is a structural artefact of algebraic target construction, independent
of location or climate. The two lowest-leakage sites (Makassar 1.72×,
Kupang 1.87×) are precisely the two sites with the highest GHI standard
deviation (0.757, 0.767 kWh/m²/day respectively). A Spearman rank
correlation confirms this systematically: ρ(GHI_SD, leakage_ratio) =
−0.903 (permutation p = 0.0007, n = 10) — a statistically significant
inverse relationship supported by sufficient statistical power at
n = 10, resolving the ambiguity present in smaller five-site samples
where the same test could not be distinguished from a coincidence of
small n.

| Location | Regime | β (GHI_anom) | SE | t-stat | p-value | Sig. |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Medan | Equatorial Wet | +0.12538 | 0.01874 | 6.692 | <0.0001 | *** |
| Pekanbaru | Equatorial Wet | +0.11167 | 0.01423 | 7.844 | <0.0001 | *** |

| Jayapura | Equatorial Rainforest | +0.07870 | 0.02235 | 3.521 | 0.00043 | *** |
| Bontang | Equatorial Maritime | +0.08743 | 0.02781 | 3.144 | 0.00167 | ** |
| Surabaya | Tropical Monsoon | +0.08849 | 0.03045 | 2.906 | 0.00366 | ** |
| Kupang | Semi-Arid Tropical | +0.07497 | 0.03186 | 2.353 | 0.01862 | * |
| Makassar | Monsoonal | +0.08356 | 0.03786 | 2.207 | 0.02732 | * |
| **Meta-Analysis (FE)** | **n=10** | **+0.10190** | **0.00667** | **15.276** | **<1e-06** | *** |
| **Heterogeneity** | **I²=0.0%** | Q=4.807 | df=9 | p_Q=0.8508 | — | — |

The fixed-effects meta-analysis confirms that GHI_anom is not only
universally significant (p < 0.03 at all ten sites) but quantitatively
stable across all six climate regimes (I² = 0.0%, p_Q = 0.851). The
pooled estimate β = +0.102 kWh/m²/day indicates that a one standard
deviation increase in monthly GHI above the site's own climatological
mean produces an additional ≈0.10 kWh/m²/day in Y_stoch, regardless of
whether the site is the semi-arid Kupang (GHI_SD = 0.767) or the
persistently cloudy Pontianak (GHI_SD = 0.373). This regime-independent
quantitative stability is the manuscript's strongest cross-site
generalisation.

| **KW between sites** | **n=10** | — | — | — | — | **H=9.000** | **p=0.4373** | **ns** |

XGBoost significantly outperforms the per-fold climatological baseline
at three of ten sites (Balikpapan p = 0.002, Bontang p = 0.010, Makassar
p = 0.037), with Balikpapan showing the strongest result (9/9 folds
positive). At Jayapura and Samarinda the pattern is directionally
positive but does not reach significance (p = 0.065, 0.082). At
Pontianak, skill scores are negative for both OLS and XGBoost — the
only site where both models underperform the mean predictor out-of-
sample. The Kruskal-Wallis test (H = 9.000, p = 0.437) does not confirm
that the across-site variation in forecastability is statistically real
rather than a consequence of the small per-site fold count (n=9 per
site).

### 4.4 SHAP Attribution — Majority- but Not Universally-Consistent

**Table 5. SHAP Rank-1 Feature — All 10 Sites**

| Location | Regime | Rank-1 Feature | Mean\|SHAP\| |
|---|---|---|---|
| Samarinda | Equatorial Maritime | GHI_anom | 0.02549 |
| Surabaya | Tropical Monsoon | T2M_x_RH | 0.02525 |
| Makassar | Monsoonal | T2M_x_RH | 0.02455 |
| Kupang | Semi-Arid Tropical | **GHI_lag12** | 0.02414 |
| Pekanbaru | Equatorial Wet | GHI_anom | 0.02162 |
| Pontianak | Equatorial Maritime | GHI_anom | 0.02022 |
| Medan | Equatorial Wet | **GHI_x_CLOUD** | 0.01872 |
| Balikpapan | Equatorial Maritime | GHI_anom | 0.01322 |
| Bontang | Equatorial Maritime | GHI_anom | 0.01320 |
| Jayapura | Equatorial Rainforest | GHI_anom | 0.01179 |

GHI_anom is the SHAP rank-1 feature at six of ten sites — a majority
but not a universal pattern. The thermal-humidity interaction (T2M×RH)
dominates at Makassar and Surabaya, the two sites with the lowest cloud
fraction and highest temperature/humidity variability after Kupang.
Two sites depart from this regime-consistent picture: at Kupang
(the site with the single highest GHI variability in the sample),
GHI_lag12 (annual persistence) rather than GHI_anom or T2M×RH ranks
first; at Medan (the highest cloud-fraction site, 89.3%), the raw-value
interaction GHI×CLOUD ranks first rather than the anomaly-based
feature. We interpret this pattern cautiously: while the broad
equatorial-vs-monsoonal contrast in Section 4.4 (GHI_anom dominant at
6/8 non-outlier sites) is consistent with a physically interpretable
mechanism, the Medan and Kupang exceptions indicate that SHAP rank-1
attribution should not be assumed constant even within a single climate
regime, and that regime alone is an incomplete predictor of feature
dominance.

---

## 5. DISCUSSION

### 5.1 Universal Leakage, Regime-Dependent Magnitude

The ten-site sample confirms that deterministic target leakage is
structural and universal — present at every location tested regardless
of climate regime — while its magnitude is demonstrably related to
local GHI variability (Spearman ρ = −0.903, permutation p = 0.0007).
The practical implication is that single-site leakage quantification
cannot be extrapolated to other climate contexts without adjustment: a
study conducted only at low-GHI-variability equatorial sites would
systematically overestimate the universal lower bound relative to one
conducted at high-variability semi-arid or monsoonal sites.

### 5.2 Meta-Analytic Synthesis: What I² = 0.0% Means

The finding that GHI_anom's coefficient is not only universally
significant but quantitatively invariant (I² = 0.0%) across six climate
regimes reflects the structural origin of the relationship: GHI anomaly
is, by construction, correlated with Y_stoch through the irradiance
term embedded in the target's physical parameterisation. The zero
heterogeneity is therefore best interpreted as confirming the internal
consistency of the stochastic target construction methodology across
sites, rather than as an independent physical finding about real PV
systems (see Limitation L1).

### 5.3 Site-Dependent Forecastability and Feature Attribution

Two independent analyses in this study (Sections 4.3 and 4.4) converge
on the same qualitative conclusion: cross-site consistency in this
domain is real but partial, not absolute. Forecastability is confirmed
at 3/10 sites (Kruskal-Wallis does not confirm the remaining variation
is systematic); SHAP rank-1 attribution is GHI_anom-dominant at 6/10
sites, with two sites (Medan, Kupang) showing patterns not predicted by
climate regime membership alone. We caution against interpreting either
result as evidence of a clean regime-based partition; the data support
"majority pattern with documented exceptions" as the most defensible
summary, not a categorical regime-forecastability or regime-attribution
rule.

---

## 6. LIMITATIONS

**(L1)** The stochastic target at all 10 sites is parameterised, not
measured against real PV plant output. The leakage ratio (Section 4.1)
is the only finding fully independent of this limitation; the meta-
analysis (Section 4.2) and attribution results (Section 4.4) should be
read as characterising the simulation's internal structure, not
confirmed properties of real PV systems.

**(L2)** n=9 walk-forward folds per site provide limited power to
formally confirm site-level forecastability differences (Kruskal-Wallis
p=0.437 is consistent with, but does not rule out, genuine but
under-powered between-site variation).

**(L3)** The Medan (GHI×CLOUD rank-1) and Kupang (GHI_lag12 rank-1)
SHAP results depart from the broader equatorial/monsoonal pattern
observed at the other 8 sites; we did not identify a clear a priori
climatic explanation for these two exceptions and flag this as an open
question for future work rather than force-fitting a post-hoc
explanation.

**(L4)** T2M×RH is a dimensionally mixed raw-value interaction (°C × %);
its dominance at Makassar/Surabaya may partly reflect the larger
absolute magnitudes of these variables at those sites rather than pure
physical signal. Normalising both components before interaction
construction is recommended for follow-up work.

**(L5)** The ten-site sample, while spanning six climate regimes,
remains confined to the Indonesian archipelago; external validity to
non-Indonesian Maritime Continent sites (Malaysia, Philippines, Papua
New Guinea) has not been tested.

**(L6)** NASA POWER's 0.5°×0.625° spatial averaging smooths sub-grid
aerosol events (e.g. Kalimantan peatland fires) at all four Kalimantan
sites, and similarly smooths any site-specific urban or coastal
micro-climate effects.

**(L7)** SARIMAX uses realised (not forecast) ONI values at every
forecast origin at all ten sites — standard practice for retrospective
evaluation, but a simplification relative to operational deployment.

---

## 7. CONCLUSION

This paper provides a ten-location empirical quantification of
deterministic target leakage in photovoltaic forecasting, spanning six
climate regimes of the Indonesian archipelago (equatorial wet,
equatorial maritime, monsoonal, tropical monsoon, semi-arid tropical,
equatorial rainforest). Three conclusions are supported at the level of
evidence this dataset permits.

**Primary (location-independent):** Deterministic target leakage is
structural and universal — R²_det ≈ 1.0 at all ten sites — but its
magnitude is systematically related to local GHI variability
(ρ = −0.903, n=10, permutation p=0.0007), spanning 1.72×–3.43× in our
sample. No single point estimate constitutes a universal lower bound;
future work should report a range conditioned on local climate
variance.

**Secondary-A (quantitatively generalised):** GHI anomaly's marginal
effect on the stochastic target is quantitatively stable across all six
regimes (pooled β = +0.102, I² = 0.0%, n=10) — the strongest cross-site
generalisation in the study, understood as a property of the simulation
methodology's internal consistency rather than a confirmed physical
finding about real PV systems (Limitation L1).

**Secondary-B (majority-consistent, not universal):** SHAP feature
dominance is GHI_anom at 6/10 sites and shifts to thermal-humidity
interaction at 2/10 lower-cloud sites, with 2/10 sites (Medan, Kupang)
showing patterns inconsistent with the broader regime-based narrative.
Forecasting practitioners should validate feature importance locally at
each new site rather than assuming regime-based transferability.

**Practice recommendation:** Multi-site PV forecasting studies reporting
leakage diagnosis should report a range of leakage ratios across
climatically diverse sites, not a single point estimate, and should
explicitly test rather than assume that feature-importance and
forecastability patterns transfer across sites even within an
apparently homogeneous climate region.

Pipeline available at: https://github.com/Jouqio/climate-aware-pv-forecasting
(auto-discovery: adding a new site requires only `data/raw/<city>.csv`,
no code changes).

## HIGHLIGHTS

*(3–5 bullet points, ≤85 characters each, per Elsevier requirements)*

- Deterministic PV target leakage is universal across 10 Indonesian sites (R²≈1.0)
- Leakage magnitude varies 1.72×–3.43×, inversely tied to local GHI variability
- Meta-analysis: GHI anomaly effect is quantitatively stable (β=+0.102, I²=0%)
- XGBoost beats climatology at only 3/10 sites; effect not confirmed between sites
- SHAP attribution is majority- but not universally-consistent across climate regimes
